clue.text: Intellect touring a hot Arab state

indicators.note: the brain goes on a tour round the other letters, enclosing them

parts.note: H = hot, as on a tap

explanation.surface: A brainy visitor tours a sweltering Gulf country.
explanation.walkthrough: Bahrain is a small island kingdom in the Persian Gulf; 'hot' fits the surface's desert heat while quietly supplying a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Bahrain is an island kingdom in the Persian Gulf, an Arab state.

clue.text: Redcoat improvised style emphasising sleekness?

indicators.note: something improvised is made up on the spot, so the letters are put together afresh

explanation.surface: A British soldier of old throws together a sleek look.
explanation.walkthrough: A redcoat was a British soldier in the red uniform of the 17th to 19th centuries; here the word is only its seven letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Art deco, the 1920s–30s design style, is known for streamlined, sleek geometric forms; the question mark flags the loose description.

clue.text: Mature writer following religious instruction

indicators.note: the writer comes after, i.e. follows, the instruction

parts.note: RI = religious instruction, the old school subject
a pen is a writer, the thing you write with

explanation.surface: An experienced author attends a class in religious studies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mature' looks like an adjective describing the writer, but it is the verb: to mature is to ripen.
explanation.definitionFit: To mature and to ripen both mean to come to full development.

clue.text: Annoying smirk one fashioned after leaving note

indicators.note: to fashion is to shape, so the letters are shaped into a new word
the note has left, so its letter is taken out

parts.note: N = note, removed from the fodder, leaving SMIRKOE

explanation.surface: Someone has put on an irritating smirk.
explanation.walkthrough: N is one of the standard abbreviations for note; take it out and the seven letters left rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both describe what gets under your skin, from the verb irk, to annoy.

clue.text: Describing route of football fans, say, in co-ordinated fashion?

definitions.text: Describing route of football fans, say
definitions.meaning: where supporters are heading on a Saturday afternoon
said of accessories chosen to go with an outfit

explanation.surface: Football supporters all dressed alike on their way to the game.
explanation.walkthrough: Both senses sit inside the one picture: fans on their way to the match, often in matching team shirts.
explanation.definitionFit: Fans head 'to (the) match'; a matching outfit is co-ordinated.

clue.text: Prompt operating link interrupted by Mike

parts.note: a machine that is operating is on

indicators.note: Mike breaks into the middle of the link

parts.note: Mike is M in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A prompt instruction to run a connection that someone called Mike keeps cutting into.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prompt' looks like a verb (to prompt an actor), but it is the adjective for punctual.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym in the punctual sense: a prompt train keeps to the timetable.

clue.text: Aspiring range having financial debts

parts.note: an ambit is a scope or range
IOUs are written promises to pay

explanation.surface: An upwardly mobile type whose ambitions have run up debts.
explanation.walkthrough: An IOU ('I owe you') is a note acknowledging a debt, so several of them are IOUS.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: both describe someone reaching for success or higher status.

clue.text: Boast before end possibly typical of a new monarch?

indicators.note: the boast comes first, ahead of the rest
the letters of END are a possible arrangement, not a fixed one

explanation.surface: Someone brags before the finale, much as a new king might.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the definition is loose: a new monarch is not always crowned at once, but being crowned is what marks one.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the coronation ceremony is the defining moment for a king or queen newly on the throne.

clue.text: First person slows Helena at work providing social service

indicators.note: the letters are busy, working themselves into a new order

explanation.surface: Helena is slowing down at her job in the caring services.
explanation.walkthrough: Meals on Wheels is the British service delivering hot meals to elderly or housebound people at home.
explanation.definitionFit: Meals on Wheels is a social service run by councils and charities.

clue.text: Part of a process shown in past episodes

indicators.note: the answer is on show inside the next words

explanation.surface: A stage of a procedure appearing in earlier instalments of a series.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer straddles the gap between the two words, which the comma-free phrase makes easy to miss.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a stage in a sequence of actions, as in 'step one'.

clue.text: Monitor open basket in need of repair

indicators.note: something broken has its parts out of order

explanation.surface: Someone is told to watch a broken, gaping basket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Monitor' reads as a noun (a screen) in the surface but is the verb, matching a three-word verb phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: to watch closely, from tabs as account records kept on someone.

clue.text: French article with time among a number in shed by building

indicators.note: the time sits among the letters of 'a number'

explanation.surface: A French text about time and numbers, filed away in a garden shed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Among' only tells you the time sits somewhere inside 'a number'; the answer's enumeration settles exactly where.
explanation.definitionFit: A lean-to is a shed built against the wall of a larger building.

clue.text: Restrictive jargon almost covering this person's relations

indicators.note: almost all of the word: its last letter is lost
the shortened jargon wraps round the rest

parts.note: this person is = I am = I'M
it = sex, as in sexual relations

explanation.surface: Someone finds narrow jargon smothering their family ties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This person's' is the contraction of 'this person is', which the setter means as I'M, not a possessive. IT for sex is a crossword standard.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: both describe what sets bounds or constraints on something.

clue.text: Firm with toffee supply around soft drink container

indicators.note: read as the adverb of supple: the toffee bends into a new shape

explanation.surface: A confectionery company supplies toffee with its soft drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supply' is not the noun but the adverb from supple, pronounced SUP-lee, which lets TOFFEE bend round P. 'Soft drink' in the surface is split: soft is P, drink joins the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by description: a jug for brewing and serving a hot morning drink.

clue.text: Female expert has the best cosmetic

parts.note: the cream is the best, as in 'cream of the crop'

explanation.surface: A woman who knows her stuff owns the finest make-up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The best' is a phrase, not an article plus adjective: the cream of anything is its finest part.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by category: a moisturiser for the skin is one of the cosmetics.

clue.text: Instant old Danny when gutted gets temperamental

parts.note: a mo = a moment, an instant

indicators.note: gutting removes the insides, leaving only the outer letters

explanation.surface: An old man called Danny, once disembowelled, turns sulky in a flash.
explanation.walkthrough: Mo is British slang for a moment, as in 'half a mo'.
explanation.definitionFit: A moody person is temperamental, with changeable moods.

clue.text: Criticism has to remain

definitions.meaning: British informal noun for harsh words aimed at someone
verb: to stay put, like glue

explanation.surface: Negative feedback is here to stay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stick' for criticism is British informal, as in 'the manager took a lot of stick'.
explanation.definitionFit: A British informal noun for flak, and a plain verb synonym for staying put.

clue.text: Dim person on board is housed in northern hotel

indicators.note: IS lives inside the other letters

parts.note: a tar is a sailor, on board ship
Hotel is H in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A slow-witted sailor is lodging in a hotel up north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dim' looks like it describes the person but is the verb: to dim or tarnish a shine. 'On board' means aboard ship, not a board game.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain verb synonym: to dull the shine of metal, or figuratively of a reputation.

clue.text: Possession when pro is playing

indicators.note: the letters are in play, moving about

explanation.surface: In sport, a team has the ball while the professional is on the field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possession' suggests the sporting sense of having the ball, which the surface leans on; the answer is the legal sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym in the legal sense: the state of having something as your own property.

clue.text: Fancy beams, say, lacking in a diplomatic residence

indicators.note: to fancy up is to rework into something new
the fodder goes without the letter that follows

explanation.surface: Ornate roof beams are missing from an ambassador's house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A' does double duty in the surface as the article before the definition, but it is the letter taken out.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by description: the official building where an ambassador lives and works abroad.

clue.text: Calm street no longer evident, producing complaint

indicators.note: the street can no longer be seen: it has gone from the word

parts.note: St = street, removed from the front

explanation.surface: A resident grumbles that the quiet road is quiet no more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Complaint' tempts toward a grievance, but here it is the medical sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Medical sense of the word: a doctor speaks of a chest complaint meaning a disorder of the body.

clue.text: Pointless dossier about posh agent, ultimately

indicators.note: the dossier goes round the other letters
only the final letter of agent is used

explanation.surface: A spy's dossier on an upper-class target turns out to be useless.
explanation.walkthrough: U for upper-class (as opposed to non-U) comes from 1950s British social commentary and is a crossword standard for posh.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: both describe an effort that can achieve nothing, from Latin futilis, leaky.

clue.text: Brother with Henry enthralled by remedy in pamphlet

indicators.note: held captive within the remedy

parts.note: H = henry, the unit of inductance

explanation.surface: A monk and Henry are gripped by a cure described in a leaflet.
explanation.walkthrough: The henry (H) is the SI unit of inductance, which is why Henry gives H.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a thin booklet of information, often promotional, stitched rather than bound.

clue.text: Take offence regarding description of a suite, it's said

indicators.note: we are told what it sounds like when spoken

parts.note: a bridal suite is the hotel room for newlyweds

explanation.surface: A hotel guest is offended by how their suite has been described.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suite' is the hotel room, not a set of furniture or music: the word that describes one is BRIDAL.
explanation.definitionFit: To bridle is to show resentment or take offence, like a horse jerking its head.

clue.text: Uniform kept by funny Finn as a joke?

indicators.note: the uniform is held inside
the letters of Finn are made to behave oddly

parts.note: Uniform is U in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A comic Finnish man dons a uniform just for a laugh.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged Finn opens as INF...N to hold U.
explanation.definitionFit: Something said in fun is said as a joke.

clue.text: Miles fined for disturbing sites with unseen hazards

indicators.note: disturbed letters are knocked out of place

explanation.surface: A man called Miles is fined for causing a disturbance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Miles' looks like M for miles, but the whole word is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Minefields are areas laid with buried mines, hazards hidden from view.

clue.text: Small jumper obtained in raffle, amazingly

indicators.note: the answer is got from inside the next words

explanation.surface: Someone wins a child's sweater in a raffle, to their surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: A jumper is British for a sweater, which is the picture; here it is something that jumps.
explanation.definitionFit: A flea is a tiny insect famous for jumping.

clue.text: Companion with a winner of award, right, in large room

parts.note: an MBE is a holder of that British honour

explanation.surface: A friend and a prizewinner sit in a great hall.
explanation.walkthrough: CH (Companion of Honour) and MBE (Member of the Order of the British Empire) are both British honours.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a hall or formal room, as in a council or debating chamber.

clue.text: James, reportedly, upset Stan, one familiar with bars?

indicators.note: Stan is knocked over, his letters rearranged
we are told how it sounds, not how it is spelt

explanation.surface: Two men, James and an upset Stan, who both know the local pubs well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bars' suggests pubs and drinkers, but these are the parallel and asymmetric bars of gymnastics.
explanation.definitionFit: A gymnast works on the parallel and uneven bars.
